title: Why Rías Baixas tastes the way it does

lede.text: Mild, wet Atlantic weather and poor granite soils. More than 96% of the grapes harvested are Albariño. It makes a lot of sugar and keeps an acidity that very few grapes in the world reach.

terms.text: The wine comes from the Condado do Tea subzone and has at least 70% Albariño and Treixadura.
A subzone name may go on the label only if all the grapes come from that subzone and the wine is made there.
A sparkling wine with 0 to 3 g/l of sugar and no sugar added after disgorging.

chapters.title: Low land beside river mouths
paras: Rías Baixas lies at 42° north and 8° west, in the provinces of Pontevedra and A Coruña.
The land rarely rises above 300 m. It is close to the sea. It follows the lower stretches of its rivers, from the Ulla in the north to the Miño in the south.
Holdings are tiny. More than 4,300 hectares are split into 22,800 plots, worked by more than 5,000 growers.

fly.label: Rías Baixas
fly.caption: A low, coastal zone, rarely above 300 m, with five subzones.

fly.label: The Miño at its mouth
fly.caption: The zone follows the lower stretches of the Miño and its tributaries, the Tea and the Louro.

chapters.title: Mild, wet and Atlantic
paras: The climate is markedly Atlantic. Temperatures are mild, between 10 °C and 25 °C. The four seasons are clearly different, and temperature swings are short.
Rain is plentiful all year, 1,300 mm. It falls much less in summer.
Topography, aspect and nearness to the sea or the rivers shade the general climate. That gives differences between the five subzones.
Spring and summer temperature and humidity make the vine very leafy.
At ripening there is not much sun, and temperatures are middling. Rain falls less, and the vines feel a slight water stress.

fly.label: Rías Baixas
fly.caption: 1,300 mm of rain a year, much less of it in summer.

fly.label: Val do Salnés
fly.caption: One of the five subzones. Each has its own shade of the climate, set by how near it is to the sea.

chapters.title: Granite, poor and sandy
paras: The land belongs to the Hercynian orogeny. Soils on granite stand out. There is also room for soils on schist and on continental alluvium from the Quaternary.
Most soils are poor in minerals that weather. They are sandy to sandy loam. Rain has washed out much of the magnesium, calcium and potassium.
They are acid, poor in nutrients and fairly shallow. They hold little water and tend to dry out in summer. Only depth limits the roots.
Growers have long worked to limit erosion and soil damage. They fertilise sensibly, and the soils respond to it very well.

chapters.title: Albariño above all
paras: Albariño is more than 96% of the grapes harvested in recent years. Other white grapes may join it. Loureira, Treixadura and Caíño Blanco are the ones that add the touches of each subzone, at no more than 30%.
Reds are under 1% of the harvest.
Yields are capped at 12,000 kg per hectare for Albariño, which gives 84 hl. Caíño Tinto is capped at 10,000 kg. Other varieties are capped at 12,500 kg.
Albariño can make more than 13% alcohol in good years. At the same time it keeps an acidity that very few grapes in the world reach.
Its wines have many aromas. Apple stands out. The wines are known more for the concentration and range of their acidity, and for their aroma, than for alcohol.
The traditional training is the pergola. It keeps the foliage away from the soil, which limits fungal disease in a humid place. It also uses sunlight better and helps manage vigour.

fly.label: Condado do Tea
fly.caption: Wine labelled Condado do Tea has at least 70% Albariño and Treixadura.
